newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iran must now show respect for law -- Bonn.
newsitem.headline: Iran must now show respect for law -- Bonn.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Saturday that Iran must show respect for international law before Bonn could discuss a fresh start in relations, shaken this week when a German court accused Iran of state terrorism.

Kinkel told the weekly Welt am Sonntag that Germany had no desire to end over a century of ties with Tehran despite ordering out four Iranian diplomats and, jointly with its European Union partners, ending a policy of "critical dialogue" with Iran.
But he said there had to be a limit to dialogue "when international law and the sovereignty of another country are massively violated".
"Iran must voice its commitment to international law and act accordingly. Then both sides must think about a fresh start," he said in an interview released ahead of publication on Sunday.

The Berlin court left Bonn little option but to act after accusing Iran's state president and religious leader on Thursday of ordering the murder of four Kurdish Iranian dissidents in a Berlin restaurant in 1992. It convicted an Iranian and three Lebanese, sentencing two of them to life for murder.

Most German commentators hailed the verdict as a judicial slap in the face for what had become an increasingly hollow foreign policy. All the EU states except Greece withdrew their ambassadors for consultations.

But Kinkel defended the "critical dialogue", championed by Bonn and agreed by the EU in 1992 under the influence of an Iranian religious edict ordering the death of British author Salman Rushdie for his book "The Satanic Verses".
The policy was supposed to keep communication channels open to encourage more pro-Western elements in the Iranian establishment, while not losing sight of human rights.

"It has achieved a number of things, for example Iran's agreement to the (United Nations) convention on chemical weapons, Iran's cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Authority, the freeing of German and other Western hostages in Lebanon, the pardoning and freeing of a German sentenced to death, a verbal agreement not to send hit squads after Salman Rushdie and a return to cooperation with the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights," Kinkel said.

Iran had campaigned to avert the court ruling, the first time that any Western judiciary had directly blamed it for any of the dozens of assassinations of exiled Iranian opposition figures since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Despite the explicit judgment, there have been few calls in Germany for economic sanctions against Iran or a complete break in diplomatic relations.
Nevertheless, there were calls on Saturday for Kinkel to take the rap for the failure of the policy he had stood for.

"Kinkel has been publicly embarrassed. His Iran policy has gone awry and he has consorted with criminals," Wilfried Penner, head of parliament's interior affairs committee, told Sunday's weekly Bild am Sonntag, according to an advance release.
"He should quit, amongst other things to give Germany the chance to forge a new Iran policy."

Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on Friday condemned the judgment and said it would hurt German and European interests, but there has been no sign so far of the violent reaction that Germany had feared.
The news weeklies Der Spiegel and Focus said German authorities had mounted a huge security operation to prevent any attacks by Moslem extremists in Germany.
Tehran Radio said a large number of demonstrators would march on the German embassy on Sunday, following a protest there on Friday by hundreds of Iranians throwing tomatoes.
